title: KnowledgeCompass AI
description:
KnowledgeCompass is an AI-powered education platform developed at Stevens Institute of Technology under Professor Edward A. Stohr. Most AI tools give generic answers. KnowledgeCompass uses curated prompts to OpenAI and Google Gemini, built on established teaching theory, to give each student a structured, personalized learning experience.
The platform has two tools:
KnowledgeExplorer: AI-guided exploration of any subject
Interactive explanations that adapt to the learner
Concept comparison and mapping
Dynamic quizzes for retention
AI tutoring, plus custom “topic explorers” users can create themselves (demo topics include Quantum Computing, Research Methods and F1 Racing)
Career Explorer: end-to-end career research and preparation
Industry and company research
AI CV and cover letter builder
Application tracker across the whole job search
Structured mock interview practice
Who it serves: students, researchers, instructors, career centers and lifelong learners. Uses range from course mastery and literature reviews to curriculum design, thesis planning and spotting struggling students early.
Impact: 600+ hours of platform usage so far (100+ on KnowledgeExplorer, 500+ on Career Explorer) and an “Excellent” user satisfaction rating.
My contributions (keep what applies, add specifics):
Designed and refined prompts to OpenAI and Gemini so outputs are accurate, structured and grounded
Built and tested features for [KnowledgeExplorer / Career Explorer]
Worked on safeguards against AI hallucination and on content quality
Analyzed usage data and student feedback to guide improvements
Created documentation, demo topic explorers and user guides
Tech: OpenAI API · Google Gemini API · Prompt Engineering ·

title: PARCEL NETWORK CONTROL TOWER
description:
One-day delivery depends on time. Each order has to make the warehouse cutoff, get picked and packed, ride an overnight truck or flight, clear a hub sort, and get out for delivery by morning. I built a Streamlit control tower that models this process across a 12-facility US network serving 20 major markets, similar to how carriers like UPS and FedEx plan next-day volume.
What it does
Optimizes fulfillment: a linear program (SciPy/HiGHS) decides, for each order, which stocking facility ships it and whether it goes by ground or next-day air. It minimizes total landed cost within facility capacity and nightly air capacity.
Models delivery time step by step: order cutoffs, pick/pack windows, linehaul speed, hub sorts, time zones, the air hub schedule and out-for-delivery times decide whether each package can arrive on time.
Uses realistic carrier pricing: distance zones 2–8, dimensional weight, fuel surcharge and residential fees.
Finds root causes: each planned miss is labeled as late order, inventory not stocked nearby, or capacity limit.
Predicts delivery risk: a Random Forest model flags packages likely to miss despite an on-time plan, from weather, hub congestion or thin slack. It recommends an action for each: upgrade to air, ship from another facility, or notify the customer.
Runs what-if scenarios: shift order cutoffs, add inventory to a facility, cut capacity, turn off air, or simulate regional weather disruptions.
AI analyst (optional): a Gemini page turns network KPIs into a plain-English operations briefing. Only aggregated metrics are sent to the model, never order-level data.
Results (simulated sample day, 3,000 orders)
Next-day on-time rate improved from 88% to 99% compared with a “ship from nearest warehouse” rule
Removed 165 packages of facility overload
Lower total landed cost including late-delivery penalties
Only about 5% of packages needed air upgrades
Pages
Executive Overview · One-Day Delivery Playbook · Network Map · Fulfillment Optimizer · Cutoffs & Time-in-Transit · Capacity & Inventory · Cost-to-Serve · SLA Risk & Exceptions · AI Network Analyst · Data & Assumptions
Tech stack
Python · Streamlit · SciPy (HiGHS linear programming) · scikit-learn · Plotly · Pandas · NumPy · Google Gemini API
Note: data is simulated; rates, speeds and cutoffs are editable planning assumptions. Users can upload their own order CSV and edit the facility network.
